newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian stocks cautious in coming week.
newsitem.headline: Asian stocks cautious in coming week.

text.p: Asian stocks are seen trading cautiously in the coming week with public holidays expected to dampen an already unenthusiastic tone in many markets.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index could lose further ground to regional markets week after posting a 57-point loss last week.
Tokyo's Nikkei 225 index is expected to rise but cap its gains at tough resistance at 19,000 points.
U.S. markets failed to provide direction on Friday, with the Dow Industrials shedding only a fraction of a two percent gain on the week. The Dow fell 11 points on Friday to close at 6,813.
Most of the smaller Asian markets are expected to fall in the coming week with the possible exception of the Philippines and Indonesia.
Manila will continue a steamroller rally that pushed the main index to record closes last week while Jakarta could consolidate or correct after recent steady gains.
Thailand will also continue to attract attention after a dropping seven-percent over the week.
Regional traders reported steady but unspectacular foreign fund flows entering the region last week from Europe and the United States.
HONG KONG - Stocks are set to approach the Chinese New Year festivities with caution, as interest rate concerns and asset allocation switches plague prices, analysts said.
A recommendation by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority that banks limit lending for the purchase of luxury properties has also left the property sector looking fragile, they added.

"The market has definitely been under pressure for the last week or so. It has run out of warrant steam, it has run out of good news and it is looking a little bit vulnerable short term." said Julian Ings Chambers, assistant director at BZW Asia.
The Hang Seng Index slipped 57.76 points, or 0.43 percent, last week to end at 13,321.79 on Friday.
TOKYO - Japan's Nikkei-225 index is expected to continue rising in the coming week after gaining 3.6 percent last week but meet tough resistance at 19,000, brokers said.

"Since the 17,000 level has been tested but was not broken through, we believe that the level will be technically supported," said Kazuo Shiogai, deputy branch manager at ING Baring Securities (Japan) Ltd.
On Friday, the Nikkei average of 225 leading issues closed at 18,330.01, up 640.65 points from January 24.

MANILA - The Philippines share market is expected to pause for breath early in the coming week after reaching record highs last week, but dealers said any profit-taking would be short-lived and the market would soon continue to march higher.
On Friday, the market surged to a record close for the second straight day, ending at 3,421.91 points. On a weekly basis, the index rose by 89.38 points, or 2.68 percent.
"(The) market may need to rest and may invite profit-taking. There may be positioning on laggards which is typical after a record run," ING Barings head of institutional sales, Louie Bate, said.
JAKARTA - Indonesian shares are likely to see a correction after their recent steady rises, brokers said.
"I think there will some correction next week because people may cash out for the Lunar New Year and Eid al-Fitr celebrations," one local broker said.
The index closed at 691.12 on Friday, up 12.2 points, or 1.8 percent, from the previous Friday.
BANGKOK - Thai stocks ended a bad week with little to look forward to as tight liquidity, currency concerns and the faltering economy continued to dominate trade, dealers said.
The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index dropped 7.13 percent in the week to 788.04 points on Friday after a one-day plunge of 3.92 percent the same day.
"The outlook of the SET next week looks bad," said Thanadech Mahapokai of Book Club Finance and Securities.
TAIPEI - Taiwan shares could test a six-year closing high in a holiday-shortened week after the central bank repeated its longstanding commitment to a "stable to loose" monetary policy, brokers said.

"Such a liquidity-driven rise should continue, but after three consecutive days of gains (as of Friday), profit-taking may emerge to offset any major gains," said Jardine Fleming Securities fund manager George Hou.
On Saturday, the index ended up 31.99 points, or 0.44 percent, at 7,315.39, up from 7,212.28 a week earlier. A 7,200-7,400 range was seen for next week.
KUALA LUMPUR - Malaysian stocks will trade easier next week after shedding 2.2 percent over the past week, dealers said.
Banking stocks will be the market's focus after two separate bank-merger proposals fell through. The banks made the announcements after the market closed on Friday.
The benchmark Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks fell 27.41 points over the week. The index shed 1.69 point to 1,216.72 on Friday.
SINGAPORE - Stocks in the city state are seen drifting lower before the Lunar New Year holidays.
"People want to close their positions because of the upcoming holidays," said broker with a local firm.
The key Straits Times Industrials index ended at 2,216.47 on Friday, down 1.15 percent over the previous week.
SEOUL - South Korean stocks are expected to move in a range between 660 and 700 points in the coming week, torn between a gloomy economic outlook and low interest rates, brokers said.
"A major rally is unlikely given an economic downturn and the Hanbo crisis," said Hyundai Securities analyst Yoo Nam-gil.
The composite index ended at 683.13 on Saturday, down 1.96 points from last Saturday's 685.11.
SYDNEY - Australian shares were seen mixed in the near term with one eye still on the Dow and nervous investors wary of the expected flow of half-yearly profit results.
The All Ordinaries index closed up six points to 2,423.7 on Friday, up 0.03 percent over the week.
WELLINGTON - New Zealand shares limped to a lower close on Friday as earnings concerns started to bite and brokers expected to see more of the same next week.
John Rattray at Ord Minnett Securities said corporate earnings were under pressure. "(High) interest rates and the currency will still gnaw away at it a bit," he said.
The NZSE-40 Capital Index ended the week at 2,386.74, down 13.53 points from the previous Friday's 2,400.27 close.
BOMBAY - Volatile Indian stocks are seen sharply lower with market sentiment hit hard after much-awaited government economic package fell far short of expectations, brokers said.
"We see a big correction ahead due to a sharp let-down on high hopes but buying by foreign funds is likely to keep the market afloat," said a dealer at a local brokerage.
The top 30-share index of the Bombay Stock Exchange ended on Friday down 3.63 percent to 3,382.47 points, a fall of 53.15 points, or 1.55 percent, on the week.

KARACHI, Pakistan - Pakistani stocks are likely to post sharp gains in the coming week as investors bet that pro-business former prime minister Nawaz Sharif will win Monday's general election, dealers said.
On Thursday, the index closed up 22.06 points, or 1.46 percent, at 1,534.21, compared to a rise of 6.92 points, or 0.48 percent, to 1,451.41 on January 23.
DHAKA - Bangladesh stocks in Dhaka maintained their rally in the week ending Thursday after recovering from a spell of corrections, but may ease in the coming week on expected profit taking.
The Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) price index rose 82.73 points at 1,962.31 in the week to Thursday.
